critic_challenges.rationale: The quote documents successful hydrocortisone replacement for a treatment-emergent endocrine toxicity (nivolumab-induced isolated ACTH deficiency), not an anticancer effect of hydrocortisone on lung adenocarcinoma. Single case report, n=1, no control; the claim's framing risks reading as efficacy against the tumor when it is supportive management of an irAE.

The quoted abstract sentence (PMID 29151505) says 'corticosteroid replacement therapy' and never names hydrocortisone; the claim's attribution of hydrocortisone rests on class inference. Also single-case, and the abstract does not appear among the supplied critic records for independent verification of the surrounding text.

'All the adverse events resolved upon treatment with hydrocortisone' covers interstitial pneumonia, hypopituitarism and a drug-induced skin disorder in one 69-year-old man; it is a single case, and resolution of pneumonitis/skin rash alongside steroid therapy cannot be assumed to be hydrocortisone-specific versus concurrent pembrolizumab withdrawal and other management.

The quoted clause only states that hydrocortisone and levothyroxine were started; it does not itself document the 'symptoms improved within one week' or pembrolizumab resumption elements of the claim, and levothyroxine co-administration confounds attribution of improvement to hydrocortisone.

The quote describes initiation of 10 mg/day hydrocortisone for ICI-associated adrenal insufficiency together with insulin for concurrent diabetes mellitus; it documents a management action, not demonstrated benefit, and 10 mg/day is a low replacement dose whose adequacy in acute adrenal insufficiency is not established by the abstract.

The quote is framed as a diagnostic/monitoring pitfall: hydrocortisone replacement unmasked diabetes insipidus with serum sodium rising to 151 mmol/L, i.e., a hazard of steroid replacement in this setting rather than a therapeutic benefit. The claim's neutral phrase 'informing glucocorticoid replacement management' understates the potential harm.

critic_challenges.rationale: This is an in-vitro mechanistic reporter-gene/mRNA induction finding in A549 cells; it demonstrates CYP3A5 mRNA upregulation (an enzyme-probe readout) rather than any antitumor or immunomodulatory efficacy in lung adenocarcinoma. The claim is also scoped as a class property of inhaled glucocorticoids ('dexamethasone and also by budenoside and beclomethasone dipropionate'), so the BDP-specific attribution is not isolated. Chosen verdict is 'stands' on the narrow biochemical statement but must not be read as therapeutic relevance for NSCLC.

The claim itself reports a rank ordering in which beclomethasone dipropionate is placed after fluticasone propionate and budesonide, i.e. BDP is not the most potent trans-repressor in A549 cells and is grouped with triamcinolone acetonide and flunisolide. This is an in-vitro comparison among a drug class, with no tumor-cell-killing, no viability, and no in-vivo or patient outcome data in lung adenocarcinoma.

The cited record directly supports a GR-dependent mechanism for BDP-induced CYP3A5 mRNA in the A549 model, so the mechanistic statement is internally supported. It remains a mechanism/induction readout in a single cell line, not evidence of efficacy or harm in lung adenocarcinoma; the same record notes BDP is metabolized by CYP3A4/CYP3A5 to inactive metabolites.

The claim states BDP is metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 to inactive metabolites, but the cited abstract also reports that CYP3A7 does not metabolize BDP and that lung cells produced only the dehydrogenated metabolite [M5] while liver cells produced hydroxylated plus dehydrogenated metabolites — so the metabolic picture is tissue-dependent and enzyme-selective, not a simple two-enzyme inactivation route. Additionally, the same record frames roughly 30% of patients as deriving little to no benefit from inhaled glucocorticoid treatment, and it is an in-vitro study, so any implication of clinical benefit for lung adenocarcinoma is unsupported.

This is a formulation-engineering claim about controlled release and superiority of BDP-loaded microparticles versus free BDP in a cytokine-release (IL-6/IL-8) assay in A549 cells — a surrogate anti-inflammatory readout, not an antitumor or patient-relevant endpoint. No tumor growth, survival, or in-vivo data are provided; the A549 line is being used as a convenient alveolar/epithelial model, and the result speaks to delivery, not to activity against lung adenocarcinoma.

This describes a solubilization/biopharmaceutics property of BDP in a simulated lung fluid, with A549 cells used only in an MTT biocompatibility assay. It provides no evidence of pharmacologic activity or efficacy in lung adenocarcinoma, and the abstract notes that exposure produced 'some metabolic changes' in the cells, i.e. the model itself responded to the medium rather than to a therapeutic effect.

critic_challenges.rationale: PMID 11698053 addresses IL-1beta-driven GM-CSF release in A549 alveolar epithelial cells, an inflammation model, not lung adenocarcinoma biology. No proliferation, survival, or tumor outcome endpoint is reported for mometasone; the claim's leap to 'relevant to suppressing pro-inflammatory signaling in lung cancer' is an inference from a single in-vitro cell line. A549 is often classified as a type II alveolar-like carcinoma line but is not a validated LUAD efficacy model.

PMID 12948397 reports a class-level effect: FK506 augmented growth inhibition of dexamethasone, methyl-prednisolone, fluticasone and mometasone alike at 10 nM. Mometasone is one of four steroids, so the finding is not mometasone-specific, and the combination partner (FK506/tacrolimus) is itself immunosuppressive — co-administration with a glucocorticoid in an NSCLC context raises an immunosuppression rather than anti-tumor concern. In-vitro growth inhibition in A549 does not establish tumor suppression in vivo.

The cited abstract (PMID 19177906) itself undercuts the framing of a preferential anti-inflammatory mechanism: it concludes that inhaled corticosteroids 'did not exhibit preferential transrepression, but had higher potencies for transactivation than for transrepression via NF-kappaB'. That is a mechanistic liability, not support for selective NF-kappaB modulation in lung cancer. The claim also asserts mometasone 'demonstrates transrepression' while the source reports mometasone within a nine-drug panel showing comparatively weaker NF-kappaB transrepression potency.

PMID 10669853 is a rhinovirus-infection model of airway inflammation in A549 cells. Suppressing ICAM-1 induction in the context of viral infection is an anti-inflammatory/antiviral-interference readout, not evidence of anti-tumor activity in lung adenocarcinoma. Extrapolating to 'NF-kappaB-dependent transcriptional programs in lung epithelial cells' as a cancer rationale is an overreach from a single viral stimulus.

PMID 18446484 is an in-vitro nanocarrier/formulation study in A549 cells explicitly framing mometasone as an 'antiasthmatic drug' with the goal of 'targeting any segment of lungs for more improved therapeutic response in other lung disorders'. The reported improvement is a delivery/AUC effect of WGA-conjugated nanoparticles, not evidence of anti-tumor efficacy; the abstract's own stated use case is asthma, not lung adenocarcinoma.

PMID 12859444 is explicitly comparative potency between two topical steroids ('have equivalent transcriptional potencies'; 'FP and MF have the same ability'). Equipotency to fluticasone is not evidence of anti-cancer activity, and the abstract notes systemic exposure at 2x10(-10) M 'with the risk of provoking concomitant adverse effects at high dosages', i.e., an effector/toxicity and systemic-liability caveat rather than a therapeutic window for cancer.

candidates.rationale: All supporting claims are A549 in-vitro anti-inflammatory/secretome or cytoprotection readouts, not LUAD/NSCLC antitumor endpoints; several are class-level or mechanism-not-efficacy (S3, S4), and critics note ceiling effects and neutral phagocyte function (PMID 42196603, 12859444). validated_supporting_claims.claim: Fluticasone propionate causes a dose-dependent, almost total inhibition of swine dust-induced IL-6 and IL-8 release from human lung epithelial A549 cells in vitro.
validated_supporting_claims.quote: Both steroids caused a dose-dependent, almost total, inhibition of swine dust-induced IL-6 and IL-8 release from epithelial cells and LPS-induced IL-6 and TNF-alpha from alveolar macrophages.

validated_supporting_claims.claim: Fluticasone propionate suppresses the epithelial secretion of pro-angiogenic mediators VEGF, IL-8, MCP-1, TNF-alpha, and IL-6 in lung epithelial cell models, supporting an effect on the epithelial secretome relevant to pulmonary microvasculature.
validated_supporting_claims.quote: An independent set of experiments showed that fluticasone propionate similarly reduced VEGF, IL-8, MCP-1, TNF-α, and IL-6, supporting a class effect of corticosteroids on the epithelial secretome.

validated_supporting_claims.claim: Fluticasone reduces cytokine-induced activation of the E-selectin promoter in stably transfected A549 lung epithelial cells, with potency greater than beclomethasone and dexamethasone, via glucocorticoid receptor-dependent mechanisms.
validated_supporting_claims.quote: The relative potencies of GC drugs as inhibitors of IL-1beta (10 pM)-stimulated ESAP-gene activation were fluticasone> beclomethasone>dexamethasone, with IC50 values of 0.13, 1.1 and 2.7 nM respectively.

validated_supporting_claims.claim: Fluticasone, along with other glucocorticoids, protects tissue cells (including A549 cells against other pore-forming toxins) against pore-forming toxin-induced cell damage, dependent on the glucocorticoid receptor and HMGCR.
validated_supporting_claims.quote: Hydrocortisone and fluticasone also protected against pyolysin-induced cell damage.

validated_supporting_claims.claim: Fluticasone (FTZ) formulations show no toxic effects on A549 cells, with cellular viability above 90%, and liposomal FTZ achieved substantially higher lung accumulation after intranasal administration in mice.
validated_supporting_claims.quote: The in vitro tests revealed no toxic effects of FTZ formulations, as cellular viability was always superior to 90% for FTZ concentrations ranging from 5 to 60 µM 72 h after incubation.

critic_challenges.rationale: Quote matches PMID 12924514 and the claim is correctly framed as an A549 in-vitro, dust-stimulated, anti-inflammatory (NF-kappaB/IL-6/IL-8) readout. It is mechanistic/anti-inflammatory, not an anti-tumor efficacy claim, and no supplied critic record contradicts it. Limitation: single transformed epithelial line, stimulus-specific, no LUAD-relevant endpoint.

PMID 10442524 itself reports only partial inhibition of IL-8 from alveolar macrophages ('The steroids only partially inhibited IL-8 release from alveolar macrophages'), so the 'almost total inhibition' wording applies strictly to epithelial cells and only to two cytokines; the claim's superlative framing is fragile. Critic record PMID 42196603 (A549, fluticasone 10^-8-10^-6 M) shows fluticasone did not change efferocytic capacity in any phagocyte tested, indicating other epithelial/immune functions are unaffected, undercutting any generalized 'protects/restores lung epithelial function' inference.

The quoted abstract text itself attributes the VEGF/IL-8/MCP-1/TNF-alpha/IL-6 reduction to 'a class effect of corticosteroids on the epithelial secretome', so the observation is not fluticasone-specific and the claim already concedes this. Additionally, cytokine/VEGF suppression in vitro is a mechanism, not evidence of anti-tumor activity in LUAD.

PMID 9371735 is a promoter-reporter (ESAP) potency comparison in stably transfected A549 cells; higher potency in repressing an adhesion-molecule promoter is a pharmacodynamic mechanism marker, not evidence of tumor benefit. Critic record PMID 12859444 (A549, AP-1/NF-kappaB/RANTES) reports fluticasone is equipotent to mometasone furoate and only 'inhibit AP-1 activity, NF-kappaB activity and RANTES release by approximately 40%' — a ceiling far below the 'almost total' inhibition framing used across these claims.

Quote matches PMID 36807406, but this is a cytoprotection assay against a bacterial pore-forming toxin (pyolysin), a co-treatment with other glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone and fluticasone), and has no LUAD/NSCLC-relevant endpoint. Critic records PMID 42196603 and PMID 42196603-context show fluticasone's in-vitro effects on phagocyte function are neutral/absent, and PMID 42196603 reports fluticasone 'significantly improved 24 h neutrophil survival and reduced early apoptosis', i.e., the direction of effect on inflammatory cell survival is pro-survival, not uniformly cytoprotective/anti-tumor.

Quote matches PMID 31658657 and the claim is narrow (absence of overt A549 cytotoxicity in a formulation study). No supplied critic record contradicts it. Note the scope is a safety/viability and lung-accumulation claim, not an efficacy claim, and viability >90% in vitro does not establish in-vivo safety or anti-tumor effect.
